title: SMTP Service Extensions
summary: Defines a framework for extending SMTP, by which a server tells a client which service extensions it supports. It introduced the EHLO greeting. It was a standards-track document, later replaced by RFC 2821.

plainLanguage.summary: A way for a mail server to say hello and list the extra things it knows how to do.

questions: how do smtp service extensions work
what is the difference between helo and ehlo
subtitle: How a mail server announces its optional features, starting with the EHLO greeting.

tldr.problem: SMTP needed new features, and the RFC wanted them added in one consistent way instead of as separate, haphazard changes.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens with the new EHLO command, and the server answers with a multiline 250 reply listing the extension keywords it supports. A registry kept by the IANA defines the keywords, and MAIL FROM and RCPT TO may carry extra parameters.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1869 is an Internet Standard that obsoleted RFC 1651, and it has itself been obsoleted by RFC 2821.

today: RFC 1869 is obsoleted by RFC 2821, which replaces it, and it in turn obsoleted RFC 1651. Its status was Internet Standard.

sections.title: Why an Extension Framework
sections.content:
SMTP had been a stable basis for relaying mail for about a decade, but the need for protocol extensions had become evident. RFC 1869 gives a single framework for all future extensions, which works without changing existing clients or servers unless the new features are actually used.

The authors warn that every extension must be scrutinized, because protocols with few options tend towards ubiquity and protocols with many options tend towards obscurity. In many cases the cost of extending SMTP will outweigh the benefit.

The framework has three parts: a new command, EHLO; a registry of service extensions; and optional parameters on MAIL FROM and RCPT TO.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail servers wanted to learn new tricks without breaking old ones. This document is the rule book for adding tricks one at a time.

sections.title: The EHLO Command
sections.content:
A client that supports extensions starts a session with EHLO instead of HELO. This amends RFC 821, so a session may now start with either command. The syntax is EHLO, a space, a domain, then CRLF.

If the server supports extensions it replies with code 250, normally a multiline reply. The first line holds the domain and an optional greeting. Each later line is a keyword with optional parameters, such as 8BITMIME. Keywords are case-insensitive. A client must not cache what it learns and must issue EHLO at the start of each session where it needs that information. After a successful EHLO, a further HELO or EHLO gets code 503.

A server that does not know EHLO answers 500 and stays in the same state, and the client may then send HELO or QUIT. A failure to list extensions returns 554. Other errors are 501 for a bad argument, 502 when it is recognised but not implemented, and 421 when the service is shutting down. After any failure or error the client should send HELO or QUIT.
sections.plainLanguage: The new hello is a longer greeting. If the other side replies "huh?", you just say the old hello instead.

sections.title: Registry, Keywords and Parameters
sections.content:
The IANA keeps a registry of SMTP service extensions, each tied to an EHLO keyword. Every registered extension must be defined in an RFC that is either on the standards track or defines an IESG-approved experimental protocol. The definition must give the extension's name, its keyword, parameter syntax, any new verbs, any new MAIL FROM or RCPT TO parameters, the effect on client and server behavior, and how much it increases the maximum command length.

Keywords starting with X are local extensions used by bilateral agreement and may not be registered. A conforming server must not offer non-X keywords that are not in a registered extension. The initial registry lists the optional RFC 821 commands SEND, SOML, SAML, EXPN, HELP and TURN.

Extensions may add parameters to MAIL FROM and RCPT TO, written as keyword=value pairs separated by spaces. This RFC defines none itself. A server that cannot handle a parameter returns 555, or 455 if it is temporarily unable to. Because parameters make lines longer, the 512 character limit now applies only to command lines without parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of tricks a server can brag about. Tricks starting with an X are private ones between friends and are not on the list.

sections.title: Received Header and Examples
sections.content:
SMTP servers are required to add a Received: field to messages. A with ESMTP clause should be added when any service extensions are used, and ESMTP was added to the registered protocol names.

The RFC shows three server behaviors. A server answering 250 with only a greeting implements just the mandatory commands. One that answers 250- lines for EXPN, HELP, 8BITMIME, XONE and XVRB implements two optional commands, one standard extension and two unregistered local ones. A server answering 500 Command not recognized: EHLO has no extensions, and the client falls back to HELO.

RFC 1869 also notes that some servers behave improperly, for example by disconnecting on EHLO. Clients are advised to watch for that and open a new connection with HELO, or to send RSET and then HELO, ignoring a failure code such as 503 in reply to the RSET.
sections.plainLanguage: Each server replies in its own way: a short hello, a long list of tricks, or "never heard of it". The client adjusts to whichever it gets.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC does not discuss security issues and is not believed to raise any beyond those already present in electronic mail and in conforming RFC 821 implementations. The EHLO reply does announce server capabilities, but the RFC says everything announced by its initial extensions could be learned by probing the verbs required to transport and deliver mail. The security implications of other extensions belong in the RFCs that define them.
sections.plainLanguage: Listing what a server can do tells nothing new, since you could find out by trying each thing anyway.
